blocks.text: New Zealand’s 1949 geodetic datum was built by surveyors, not by an electronic computer. The first-order triangulation was completed in 1942; astronomical observations established the datum in 1949. LINZ records 284 first-order stations in the original adjustment. Those observations and network adjustments supplied a national control framework before electronic computing became routine.

blocks.text: NZGD49 was static: the coordinates of its defining stations remained fixed. LINZ notes distortions of up to five metres in parts of the network. A later programme could return a consistent answer and still inherit the limitations of the observations and adjustments it started from.

blocks.text: Electronic computers made it practical to repeat coordinate reductions and transformations across an established network. They helped surveyors compare new observations with known control and process more points consistently, while decisions about the reference and adjustment remained part of the survey work.

blocks.text: For GIS work, keep datum and projection separate. NZGD49 defines the geodetic reference; NZMG converts positions to a map grid. A wrong transformation can shift otherwise precise coordinates, so preserve the source reference and check known control before treating a recalculated layer as aligned.
